draft.title: The Bohr model
card: In the Bohr model, electrons orbit the nucleus only at certain fixed energy levels. An electron in one of these levels does not radiate energy.
An electron can jump to a higher level only by absorbing a photon. The photon's energy must equal the difference between the two levels.
When an electron falls to a lower level, it emits a photon. The photon's energy is the difference between the levels: E = hf, where h is Planck's constant and f is the frequency.
Hydrogen has only certain energy gaps, so it emits only certain frequencies of light. This gives a line spectrum of separate bright lines, not a continuous band.
draft.remember: Fixed energy levels mean fixed photon energies, so hydrogen gives separate spectral lines.

a.q: Why does the light from excited hydrogen gas form separate lines, not a continuous band?
opts: Electron jumps release only photons of certain energies
Electrons spiral inward and release energy gradually
Hydrogen atoms release light of every frequency in turn
Electrons absorb photons of any energy they receive
a.why: Electrons can only move between fixed levels, so each fall gives a photon of one set energy and one set frequency. A spiral inward would give a continuous range of energies, but the Bohr model does not allow this.
a.clue: Think about which energy gaps are allowed.

b.q: In a hydrogen atom, an electron falls from level 3 to level 2, and then from level 2 to level 1. The gap from level 2 to level 1 is larger than the gap from level 3 to level 2. Which statement is correct?
opts: The second jump emits a photon of higher frequency
The second jump emits a photon of lower frequency
Both jumps emit photons of the same frequency
The first jump emits a photon of higher energy
b.why: Photon energy equals the gap between levels, and E = hf, so a larger gap gives a higher frequency. The second jump has the larger gap, so its photon has the higher frequency. The first jump has the smaller gap, so its photon has less energy.
b.clue: Compare the two gaps, then link energy to frequency.

a.best: Electron jumps release only photons of certain energies

b.best: The second jump emits a photon of higher frequency

problems.detail: The card says an electron can jump to a higher level 'only by absorbing a photon'. Atoms can also be excited by collisions, for example with electrons in a discharge tube (Franck–Hertz) or by heating. That is how the 'excited hydrogen gas' in question a is usually excited. Change it to say absorbing a photon is one way an electron can jump up.

proposal.title: The Bohr model
card: In the Bohr model, electrons orbit the nucleus only at certain fixed energy levels. An electron in one of these levels does not radiate energy.
One way an electron can jump to a higher level is by absorbing a photon whose energy equals the gap between the levels. Collisions, such as in a heated gas, can also raise it.
When an electron falls to a lower level, it emits a photon. The photon's energy is the difference between the levels: E = hf, where h is Planck's constant and f is the frequency.
Hydrogen has only certain energy gaps, so it emits only certain frequencies of light. This gives a line spectrum of separate bright lines, not a continuous band.
proposal.remember: Fixed energy levels mean fixed photon energies, so hydrogen gives separate spectral lines.
